title: Seeing God
hook: Catholic and Orthodox writers speak of seeing God face to face as our joy
tomorrow: Not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, new creation: the holy city coming down, not souls floating up. Your line was heaven comes down.

Hold up a spoon and look into the bowl of it. There you are, upside down, blurred, the color off. It's you, but not clearly. Paul reaches for a picture like that when he writes to Corinth about what comes at the end: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Behind that line stands an old refusal. Moses, who had seen the burning bush and the sea split open, once asked God, "I beseech thee, shew me thy glory." And God answered, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live."

First, the refusal. God sets Moses in a cleft of the rock, covers him with a hand while the glory passes by, and lets him see from behind. Not the face. Moses has to be hidden to be kept safe. Second, the promise. Jesus says, "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God." The letter of John says, "we shall see him as he is." And Paul's glass, in the King James, is a mirror. Some readers say God is glimpsed now only in reflections, in scripture, in other people, in a sunset, never straight on. Then, face to face. Third, the name. Catholic theology calls this the beatific vision, from the Latin for the seeing that makes blessed. Seeing God isn't a reward handed out alongside other rewards; it is the joy itself. Thomas Aquinas, among others, taught that human longing finally comes to rest there. Orthodox writers speak of beholding the light of God, the light the disciples saw on the mountain when Jesus was transfigured, and of sharing in God's life. Protestant hymns sing of seeing Christ face to face. The churches haven't only used different words here; they have argued. Orthodox theology holds that God's essence stays beyond any creature, and the saints see and share God's uncreated light; Catholic theology speaks of seeing God's essence. Both place the joy in seeing God. Fourth, the seeing goes both ways. Paul finishes his sentence: "then shall I know even as also I am known." In Paul's line, being known comes first.

Close your eyes. If you pray, bring to mind the hope of seeing God's face, without picturing any features, only the sense of being looked at with love, and of looking back; if you don't, bring to mind the face of someone who has loved you well, and let yourself be seen by it. Either way, don't perform: just be seen.
Beatific vision. From the Latin, the seeing that makes blessed: the hope of seeing God face to face, as the joy itself.
Your line: face to face. No more blurred spoon. Same time tomorrow.
